newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Women's issue threatens Afghan aid.
newsitem.headline: Women's issue threatens Afghan aid.

text.p: Crucial western aid to war-ravaged Afghanistan, one of the world's poorest countries, could end unless Kabul's new purist Islamist rulers change their attitude to women working, aid officials said on Friday.
"I think we all agree that we should do the winter programme at any cost because there is a highly vulnerable population facing severe weather with few resources," said one.

"But our mandates, whether you're talking about U.N. agencies or NGOs (non-governmental organisations), do not allow gender discrimination and it could come to the stage where we have to close down our operations," he said.
Another said the women's issue could threaten funding for the programmes, mostly supplied by Western governments.
An annual appeal for aid to Afghanistan is due to be launched in December. "I can't see Western governments being forthcoming if this situation goes on," the official said.
The aid officials said at least 200,000 people in Kabul, a city of an estimated 1.2 million people, received daily help, mainly food, from Western-sponsored programmes.

Many hospitals and clinics get supplies, salaries and doctors from Western agencies, which are also involved in supplying water and sanitation to the dusty city of Kabul and other areas of Afghanistan.

The officials said aid groups were meeting on Friday and Saturday to work out a coordinated approach to the new Taleban rulers, whose movement has captured some three-quarters of Afghanistan since it was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan two years ago.

There was hope, with some members of the six-man council set up after the Taleban took Kabul a week ago expressing understanding of the attitude of aid groups which are often dependent on Afghan women, especially those whose projects are designed to help women and children.

Another aid official said no group wanted to confront the government over the women's issue but said most projects had ground to a halt because women workers were afraid to turn up after the Taleban decreed that women should not appear in public without wearing the all-embracing burqa (veil).
"Everyone is trying to get over this problem, But it's not business as usual. Most NGO programmes have ground to a halt," he said.

The only programmes still working were medical, but even those were only sputtering along because few women were turning up at hospitals and clinics for treatment, added the official, who like the others asked not to be identified.
"Most of us want to go back to the situation as it was before, when women worked in the most Islamic manner possible. But in our work, it's not possible to separate men and women completely."
The aid officials all agreed Western agencies should work, no matter what, through the winter to help a population impoverished by war and destruction.

"Our feeling is that most of those who could afford to leave have left. Most of those still here have nowhere to go or no means to leave, so you by and large have a population highly vulnerable to winter," said a third aid official.
"You have children without proper winter clothes, without shoes facing a harsh cold winter with lots of snow and not enough nourishment to stand it. We simply cannot leave them to it," he said.
"It also gives us the opportunity to prove to the Taleban that we are what we say we are: efficient organisations which can deliver help."

The officials said part of the problem was that Taleban decrees on women in relatively cosmopolitan Kabul were being enforced by fighters from the conservative countryside, where few women are seen by any but their closest relatives.
There have been several reports of women being beaten up in the streets by Taleban fighters for offending the dress code in a city where educated women often wore jeans or dresses in public.
Taleban leaders had assured aid groups that the situation would improve once most of these fighters had been moved out of the city, but had given no time frame, the aid officials said.
"But until they go, or until policy is publicly changed, we can't bring women to work because they would be in danger," said one.
"We'll try and work out a non-confrontational solution and we'll certainly go on through the winter. But unless things change, I don't see any way we can carry on after that."
